REPORT
Date October 12, 19 31.

Subject (in full) Alleged smuggling of four students of Chinan University into Java.

Made by D.I.Kuh Paohwa Forwarded by A.B. Km a1.

With reference to the inquiry of October 5, 1931 from
the Netherlands Consulate-General, concerning the alleged
smuggling of four students of the Chinan University into
Java, I have to report that diligent inquiries made in
connection with this matter have, so far, failed to confirm
the information supplied by P.H. Pitterson. Discreet
inquiries among the students of the Chinan University
have also been unsuccessful.
Regarding P.H. Pitterson, this individual, who is
undoubtedly a shady character, left the Hung Fah (鸿发)
hotel, No. 111 Boulevard de Montigny on September 30, 1931
and since then his whereabouts have become obscure. Enquiries
among his friends in the various schools and at his usual
haunts have failed to disclose his present address.

Kuh Pao hwa
D. I.

Officer i/c Special Branch.

Mr Yu, Please reply sending
a copy of the above report.

K.H. Pitterson.

K.H. Pitterson alias Sun Kheng Hoon alias Chu Wen
( 24 ), is a native of Menado, Celebes, Dutch East Indies.
He claims to be a musician by profession and also is
capable of singing and dancing. He speaks English rather
well and has a slight knowledge of Fukienese. His father
is said to be a merchant somewhere in Java, with branch
offices in Hongkong and Amoy and is reported to be wealthy.
Pitterson says he receives from his father a monthly remit-
tance varing from $200 to $500 which he spends in gambling
at the Canidrome.

I noticed more than thirty pawn tickets in his
possession, which were for musical instruments, a diamond
ring and a gramophone etc.

He is residing in Hung Fah Hotel (      ), No.111
Boulevard Montigny, room 19, but his telegraph address is
either 303 or 310 Rue Bourgeat for communication with his
father. He used to stay at his uncle's house, at No. 218
Avenue Foch, where he is keeping his clothes. He removed to
the hotel on account of restriction as his uncle insisted
that he be at home by 10 p.m. every night. His uncle does
not know that he is staying in the hotel, as he told him that
he lives in School, while to his father he wrote that he is
in hospital suffering from illness.

On 22.9.31 he received about $200 from his father on
the strength of his alleged sickness. Once he took me to
a pawnshop on Woosung Road, and after giving me some money, asked me
to redeem a pair of shoes, a velvet hat and a suit of clothes,
which had been pawned for $86. At the time I was redeeming
these things, he stood outside the shop, and
the master of the shop informed me that these articles had
been pawned by a tall Cantonese, not by a Pitterson.

(2)

As soon as he received the redeemed clothing he took
the tram and proceeded back to his hotel.
He said that he is very well known around the
Shanghai dance halls, cafes etc., for his numerous fights.
Once when I asked him about the possibility of
travelling to Java without a passport, he told me how he had
helped some Chinese students to reach Java without the
passports.
He usually put such passengers in the cook's galley
on one of the Dutch steamers plying between Shanghai and
Java, and the cook keeps them there until the boat enters
the port. After a waiting a couple of hours, when every-
thing is quiet, the cook sends them ashore to a certain
address posing as members of the crew. This method of
transportation is cheaper than travelling on a ticket and
he says he has already sent four students of Chinan
University.
He asked me whether I would like to go Java or Amoy
as he could fix everything for me.

a letter which I received from a certain Sieh Jih-kwan

SHANGHAI. 8th May 1931.

Sir,

I have the honour to inform you that a certain Soei
Keng-hoen (孫慶雲) alias Sun Kheng-hoon alias Ch'ou
Wen (周文) alias K.H. Pitterson, born at Menado (Celebes,
N.E.I.) about 23 years of age, applied from time to time
to this Consulate General for financial assistance.

It appears that in stead of devoting himself to his
schoolwork he wasted his time and money on everything
but his studies.

In 1927 he obtained through the intermediary of this
Consulate General a substantial sum of money from his
father to pay his debts.

In 1928 further assistance was refused to him on
account of his misbehaviour in this office.

In the beginning of this year he approached the Con-
sulate again, telling all sorts of lies and asking again
for financial assistance from home.

It appears that during the greater part of last year
he lived at the Tung Nan Hotel, 563 North Szechuen Road,
leaving there an unpaid bill of more than $ 300.--. He
gave his Netherlands' passport to the manager by way of
security, stating to the Consulate that he had lost it.

His nerves seemed to be overstrained and he was and
still is in a very irritable state of mind.

This Consulate General advised his father, through the
